General Question About Bike Touring

What is Bike Touring, and What Are the Different Types?

Bike touring is traveling long distances by bicycle, blending cycling with backpacking or traveling. It ranges from "credit-card touring" (carrying minimal gear and staying in hotels) to self-supported "bikepacking" (carrying a tent and camping off-grid). We offer sturdy gravel and touring bikes built to handle it all.

How Hard is it to Learn Bike Touring?

If you know how to ride a bicycle, you can go bike touring! The biggest adjustment is simply getting used to the extra weight of your gear and learning to pace yourself. We highly recommend starting with a shorter "sub-24-hour" overnight trip to test out your setup and get a feel for the ride.

How Does a Touring Bike Compare to a Regular Mountain Bike?

Touring bikes are designed for comfort and load-carrying over long distances. They feature a more relaxed geometry so you can ride comfortably all day, drop bars or flat bars with multiple hand positions, and reinforced frames with special mounting points for racks, panniers, and extra water bottles.

Why Do People Get Into Bike Touring?

It’s the ultimate way to slow down and see the world. Bike touring combines the physical reward of cycling with the thrill of self-reliant exploration. It allows you to connect with nature, take in the scenery at a human pace, and experience Colorado in a way you simply can't from inside a car.

Where Can I Tour in Colorado, and Do I Need Permits?

Colorado is a world-class destination for cycling! You can ride the paved paths around Summit County, tackle the scenic paved stretches of the Copper Triangle, or hit the unpaved Great Divide Mountain Bike Route. While you don't need permits to ride the roads, you do need to check if your planned campsites along the route require advance reservations or backcountry permits.

What Do I Need to Wear?

Comfort is key. Padded cycling shorts (a chamois) are highly recommended for long days in the saddle. Dress in breathable, moisture-wicking layers, and always pack a reliable waterproof windbreaker or rain jacket—mountain weather can change rapidly at elevation!

How Do You Pack and Balance Gear on a Touring Bike?

Balance is crucial for a smooth ride. You want to keep the heaviest items (like food, water, and tools) as low as possible and centered in a frame bag or the bottom of your panniers. Lighter, bulkier items (like your sleeping bag and spare clothes) should go in your seat pack or handlebar bag.

How Does Riding a Fully Loaded Bike Feel?

A loaded bike will feel heavier, slower to accelerate, and less "twitchy" than an unloaded bike. You'll need to give yourself extra stopping distance on descents, and you'll want to shift your gears early and often when approaching hills. It only takes a few miles to adapt to the new momentum!

How Do I Handle Steep Climbs on a Loaded Bike?

Patience and gearing! Shift into your easiest "granny gear" before the climb gets steep, stay seated to maintain traction, and find a steady, sustainable pedaling rhythm. There is absolutely no shame in getting off and walking your bike if a mountain pass gets too tough—it’s all part of the adventure.

Do I Need to Camp, or Can I Stay in Hotels?

It’s entirely up to you! You can do "self-supported" touring where you carry a tent, sleeping bag, and stove to camp under the stars. Alternatively, you can do "credit-card touring" where you carry just a change of clothes and sleep in lodges, Airbnbs, or hotels along your route.

What Types of Terrain Can Your Touring Bikes Handle?

Our rental fleet is equipped with durable, wide tires that provide excellent traction and comfort. They are designed to confidently handle paved highways, scenic greenway paths, packed dirt roads, and rugged gravel trails.

What Happens if I Get a Flat Tire on the Road?

Flats are part of the journey! We can include a comprehensive repair kit (spare tubes, tire levers, a pump, and a multi-tool) with your rental. If you are heading out on a multi-day trip, we highly recommend knowing the basics of how to change a bicycle tube before you hit the road.
